chapters.title: The Friction
chapters.teaserText: A transfer should feel like a promise-not a gamble.
chapters.deepDiveHtml:
Where it began

In 2011, Remitly co-founder Matt Oppenheimer was living in Nairobi, Kenya, working in mobile and internet banking for Barclays. It was there, watching people around him try to receive money from family working abroad, that he saw the problem up close and not as a statistic, but as something playing out in the lives of people he knew.

The friction, specifically

People sending money internationally had to wait a long time, and on top of that they faced high fees, unfair exchange rates, slow transfers, weak security, and no real guarantee their money would even arrive. Every transfer meant navigating a system built for the convenience of intermediaries-banks, agents, wire services-not for the people actually relying on it.

Third parties like banks and remittance companies were taking at least 8-10% in service fees on every transfer and money was being quietly deducted from what was meant to reach a family on the other side of the world.

The True Cost: For example, on a standard $200 transfer, traditional services often siphoned off $16 to $20 (8-10%) in hidden fees and markups. Remitly introduced a digital model that reduced this to just a few dollars, leaving significantly more money in the pockets of the families who needed it.

Who felt it most acutely

The people caught in this system were immigrants in the U.S. and U.K. supporting families back home in countries like the Philippines, India, and El Salvador. These weren't occasional transactions... they were a lifeline. A missed or delayed transfer wasn't an inconvenience; it could mean a family going without groceries, school fees, or medicine that month. Compounding the problem: many of the people receiving this money didn't have access to formal banking at all.

The moment it clicked

Oppenheimer didn't set out with a ready-made solution he simply couldn't unsee the problem. His own advice to future founders: fall in love with a problem you want to solve, not with a specific solution.

chapters.title: The Founder(s)
chapters.teaserText: One observed problem became a three-founder mission.
chapters.deepDiveHtml:
Matthew Oppenheimer (CEO)

Chairman and co-founder of Remitly (NASDAQ: RELY). As founder and CEO over 15 years, he grew the company from inception to $75 billion in volume, $1.6 billion in revenue, and to profitability across 170 countries and serving over 9 million customers.

Josh Hug (COO)

Co-founded Remitly alongside Matt, bringing strong operational leadership to the company's early tech and product development.

Shivaas Gulati

He co-founded Remitly, helping scale the company from inception to its $8B IPO on Nasdaq, and gaining deep experience in product, technology, and customer-driven growth at global scale.

chapters.title: The Business Model
chapters.teaserText: Two small slices of every transfer built a large network.
chapters.deepDiveHtml:
1. Executive Summary

Remitly is a leading digital-native cross-border financial services provider primarily engineered for immigrants and expatriate communities globally. Operating across a scalable asset-light infrastructure, Remitly disrupts traditional, high-cost brick-and-mortar remittance services (e.g., Western Union, MoneyGram) by leveraging a proprietary mobile-first platform.

2. Core Value Proposition

Remitly delivers a dual-sided value proposition addressing the asymmetric needs of senders and receivers. For Senders (Immigrants): Eliminates absolute dependency on retail branches by offering an intuitive mobile app/web interface. Senders receive completely transparent pricing, highly competitive exchange rates, and explicit delivery time guarantees. For Receivers: Provides localized flexibility through an omnipresent omnichannel disbursement network (direct bank deposits, mobile wallet credits, home delivery, cash pickup).

3. Target Customer Segments

Cross-Border Migrant Workers sending critical, non-discretionary baseline capital to support family living expenses in emerging economies. And Underbanked Receivers who frequently lack traditional institutional banking access.

4. Monetization & Revenue Architecture

Remitly utilizes a dual-engine monetization mechanism. Tiered Transaction Fees: Express Tier (higher flat fee/percentage, funded via debit/credit for instant deployment) vs Economy Tier (low or zero fees, funded via bank transfers requiring 3-5 days). Foreign Exchange (FX) Spread Markup: Generates margins from the spread between wholesale institutional FX interbank market rates and the retail exchange rate.

7. Strategic Defensibility (Moats)

High Network Effects & Switching Costs, Proprietary Risk Management Engine, and Asymmetric Regulatory & Licensing Capital across thousands of international corridors.

chapters.title: Geography & Scale
chapters.teaserText: A Seattle pin became a six-continent payments network.
chapters.deepDiveHtml:
Where it started

Remitly was founded in Seattle, Washington in May 2011 (originally as BeamIt Mobile, renamed Remitly in August 2012). It got its first money-transmitter license in April 2012, and launched its first live corridor the US-to-Philippines transfer service, in April 2013, followed by US-India and US-Mexico corridors in 2014-2015.

Where it went

From that single corridor, Remitly built out a global send-and-receive network. As of 2026, it lets customers send from more than 175 countries, supporting transfers in over 100 currencies via bank deposit, cash pickup, mobile wallet, home delivery, and debit card channels. The company now operates roughly 5,600 total payment corridors. Its largest and most concentrated receive markets are India, Mexico, and the Philippines.

Expansion continued in 2025-2026

WhatsApp Send launched in the UK, Canada, and Spain, letting users there send to 14 receiving countries. Remitly Business (its B2B product) went live in Canada in May 2026. It also expanded outside pure remittance in 2023 by acquiring Rewire, strengthening its footprint in the Middle East.

chapters.title: Status Today
chapters.teaserText: The heartbeat changed rhythm; it did not slow down.
chapters.deepDiveHtml:
Still running - and doing great.

  • ✅ Public company: listed on NASDAQ (ticker: RELY) since September 2021, after raising ~$300M in its IPO
  • 💰 Real money now: $452.8M revenue in Q1 2026 alone, up 25% from last year. Net income of $49.1M, up a massive 332% YoY
  • 📈 Turned profitable: 2025 was its first full year of GAAP profit. For over a decade before that, it was growing fast but losing money-the classic startup playbook. Not anymore.
  • 🌍 Bigger than ever: 9.6 million active customers moving $22 billion+ every quarter across roughly 5,000 money-transfer corridors worldwide.
  • 👔 Leadership handoff: In Feb 2026, co-founder Matt Oppenheimer stepped down as CEO and became Chairman instead. Sebastian Gunningham now runs the company day-to-day.
  • 🚀 Still pushing forward: rolled out business payment tools, expanded transfers over WhatsApp, and even made itself accessible inside ChatGPT.

What it means: Remitly did exactly what it set out to do in 2011 build a faster, cheaper way to send money abroad and won. It out-competed legacy players like Western Union and MoneyGram at their own game. It's a stable, profitable, publicly-traded company now focused on staying ahead of newer competitors.
